definition: The third generation of the AMBA AXI protocol, featuring five independent channels, out-of-order completion, and bursts up to 16 beats. Includes the WID signal for write data interleaving.
The fourth generation of the AMBA AXI protocol. Expands bursts up to 256 beats, removes the WID signal (forbidding write data interleaving), and adds QoS and Region support.
A simplified subset of AXI4 designed for basic control registers. Removes burst capability, exclusive accesses, and most sideband attributes. All transactions are exactly one beat.
A non-memory-mapped variant of AXI designed for high-speed, continuous data streams (like video or networking). Uses only a ready/valid handshake and payload; has no address channel.
A complete operation (read or write) on a bus, encompassing the initial address phase, the transfer of the data payload (burst), and the final response.
The entire data payload associated with a single address request in a transaction.
A single data transfer within a burst. If the data bus is 4 bytes wide, a 64-byte burst takes 16 beats to complete.
The two-way VALID/READY mechanism used by AXI to transfer information. The transfer only occurs when both VALID (from source) and READY (from destination) are HIGH on a rising clock edge.
A transaction for which the address has been issued, but the final data/response has not yet been received. AXI supports multiple outstanding transactions simultaneously to achieve high throughput.
The independent channel used by a master to initiate a write transaction and provide control attributes. (AWVALID, AWREADY, AWADDR, etc.)
The independent channel used by a master to transfer the write payload to the slave. (WVALID, WREADY, WDATA, etc.)
The independent channel used by a slave to confirm the success or failure of a completed write transaction. (BVALID, BREADY, BRESP, etc.)
The independent channel used by a master to initiate a read transaction and provide control attributes. (ARVALID, ARREADY, ARADDR, etc.)
The independent channel used by a slave to return the requested read payload and status to the master. (RVALID, RREADY, RDATA, etc.)
Write Address Valid (Master -> Slave). Indicates that valid write address and control information is available.
Write Address Ready (Slave -> Master). Indicates that the slave is ready to accept a write address.
Write Address. The initial physical memory address for the write burst.
Write Burst Length. Defines the exact number of beats in a write burst. Length = AWLEN + 1.
Write Burst Size. Defines the size in bytes of each data beat within the write burst (encoded as a power of 2).
Write Burst Type. Determines how the address is calculated for subsequent beats in the write burst (FIXED, INCR, WRAP).
Write Lock Type. Provides information about the atomic characteristics of the write transaction.
Write Cache Type. Specifies the memory type and how the write transaction must progress through the interconnect.
Write Protection Type. Specifies the privilege level and secure nature of the write transaction.
Write Quality of Service (AXI4 only). Used to prioritize write transactions within a system interconnect.
Write Region Identifier (AXI4 only). Permits a single slave interface to manage multiple logical regions of memory.
Write Address ID. The identification tag for the write address group. Used for out-of-order tracking.
Write Valid (Master -> Slave). Indicates that valid write data is available.
Write Ready (Slave -> Master). Indicates that the slave can accept the write data.
Write Data. The actual data payload to be written.
Write Strobes. One bit per byte lane in WDATA. Indicates which byte lanes contain valid data.
Write Last. Asserted HIGH by the master during the final beat of a write burst.
Write Data ID (AXI3 only). An identification tag for the write data beat, allowing data interleaving. Removed in AXI4.
Write Response Valid (Slave -> Master). Indicates that a valid write response is available.
Write Response Ready (Master -> Slave). Indicates that the master can accept a write response.
Write Response. A 2-bit status code indicating the success or failure of the entire write transaction (OKAY, EXOKAY, SLVERR, DECERR).
Response ID. The identification tag for the write response, matching the original AWID.
Read Address Valid (Master -> Slave). Indicates that valid read address and control information is available.
Read Address Ready (Slave -> Master). Indicates that the slave is ready to accept a read address.
Read Address. The initial physical memory address for the read burst.
Read Burst Length. Defines the exact number of beats in a read burst. Length = ARLEN + 1.
Read Burst Size. Defines the size in bytes of each data beat within the read burst (encoded as a power of 2).
Read Burst Type. Determines how the address is calculated for subsequent beats in the read burst (FIXED, INCR, WRAP).
Read Lock Type. Provides information about the atomic characteristics of the read transaction.
Read Cache Type. Specifies the memory type and how the read transaction must progress through the interconnect.
Read Protection Type. Specifies the privilege level and secure nature of the read transaction.
Read Quality of Service (AXI4 only). Used to prioritize read transactions within a system interconnect.
Read Region Identifier (AXI4 only). Permits a single slave interface to manage multiple logical regions of memory.
Read Address ID. The identification tag for the read address group. Used for out-of-order tracking.
Read Valid (Slave -> Master). Indicates that valid read data is available.
Read Ready (Master -> Slave). Indicates that the master can accept the read data.
Read Data. The returned data payload from the slave.
Read Response. A 2-bit status code provided with every beat of read data, indicating success or failure.
Read Last. Asserted HIGH by the slave during the final beat of a read burst.
Read ID. The identification tag for the read data group, matching the original ARID.
Generic term for the 4-bit ARCACHE or AWCACHE signal, which defines memory type (bufferable/cacheable) and basic ordering constraints.
Generic term for the 3-bit ARPROT or AWPROT signal, defining privilege (User/Privileged), security (Secure/Non-secure), and instruction vs. data access.
Generic term for the 4-bit ARQOS or AWQOS signal (AXI4 only), used for Quality of Service prioritization in interconnects.
Generic term for the 4-bit ARREGION or AWREGION signal (AXI4 only), used to identify logical decode regions for a slave.

The ability for a slave to return data or responses in a different order than the requests were received, improving throughput by not stalling on long-latency requests. Only permitted for transactions with different IDs.
The core AXI ordering rule: transactions with the same ID must complete in the exact order they were issued. Transactions with different IDs have no ordering guarantees.

An AXI constraint stating that one burst must not cross a 4 KB address boundary. Compare the address bits above bit 11 for the first and final transferred byte. The rule keeps one accepted burst within one decode/routing region; it is not a virtual-memory page-fault rule.
An interconnect architecture that uses a matrix of switches to allow multiple masters to communicate with multiple slaves simultaneously, provided they are not targeting the same slave.

In AXI4, the AxQOS signals allow masters to indicate the priority of a transaction. Interconnect arbiters use these signals to prioritize critical traffic (like real-time video) over bulk data transfers.
Global clock signal. All signals are sampled on the rising edge of ACLK.
Global reset signal. Active-LOW. Must be driven synchronously for de-assertion.
Exclusive Access Okay. A response indicating that an exclusive access (read or write) was successful. Illegal for FIXED bursts.
